previous_admission_summary.summary_paragraph: A woman with type 1 diabetes, gastroparesis, and a history of anxiety was admitted for severe nausea and vomiting, uncontrolled blood glucose, and hypertensive urgency. She presented with diabetic ketoacidosis and metabolic alkalosis, requiring IV insulin, fluids, and antiemetics. Her condition improved with treatment, and she transitioned to a regular diet. Psychiatry recommended switching from Ativan to Klonopin for better long-term management of anxiety-related nausea. She was discharged home in stable condition with medication changes and follow-up plans for psychiatry and diabetes care.

Reglan, Ativan, Compazine, NPO and IV fluids. As she did not

her nausea and vomiting improved her diet was advanced and she 
tolerated a full liquid diet prior to discharge.

2. Lactic acidosis: Likely secondary to dehydration due to 
vomiting. Lactate improved s/p IV fluids and her gap closed.

3. Hypertension, benign: Consistent with elevated blood 
pressures during prior admissions, thought to be brought on by 
nausea and vomiting. Patient is also likely to be missing home 
doses of Lisinopril given persistent problems with vomiting. 
Blood pressures stabilized with treatment of nausea and 
re-institution of Lisinopril.

4. Anemia: Patient to undergo outpatient colonoscopy in ___ 
Hct here elevated above prior discharge value, likely due to 
hemoconcentration in setting of dehydration. It decreased with 
volume resuscitation to 28, consistent with her hematocrit at 
her prior discharge, and remained stable at this level. 

5. Anxiety, depression: Unable to assess mood in setting of 
ongoing vomiting. Patient had not yet followed up with 
outpatient psychiatry and was encouraged to do so. Home 
medications were continued.

6. DMI, uncontrolled, with complications: Patient was continued 
on her home Lantus and sliding scale; Levemir was switched to 
Lantus and given at a reduced dose of 10u as the hospital does 
not carry Levemir, but she was instructed to resume her home 
regimen at discharge. She was instructed to use her bedtime 
sliding scale if she is not able to take PO's, and to take her 
usual sliding scale immediately after meals for the next few 
days to ensure she keeps her meals down in an effort to prevent 
hypoglycemia. She had no episodes of hypoglycemia during this 
hospitalization.
